title: Home Is a Verb
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 16 of 40
content:
Toph’s ankle healed before any of us stopped hovering.

This was unfortunate, because Toph’s patience with hovering had expired approximately three minutes after the injury.

By the time Katara declared the bone sound, Toph had already planned a celebration involving three sparring partners, a barrel of something she refused to identify, and “a responsible amount of property damage.” Katara cancelled the barrel. Aang cancelled the property damage. I made the mistake of asking what counted as responsible.

“Less than a wall,” Toph said.

“That is not a unit of measurement.”

“It is if you’re fun.”

She planted both bare feet in the courtyard and bent a waist-high ring of stone around herself. The earth answered with a clean, satisfying crack. Relief passed over her face so quickly I might have missed it before I knew her.

Aang did not miss it. Neither did Katara.

Nobody said anything sentimental.

This, more than anything, proved we loved her.

That evening we ate outside because Toph wanted ground under her feet and Aang wanted sky over his head. Katara brought soup. I brought the council packet I had promised not to touch until morning and then spent half of dinner pretending it had appeared beside my elbow by accident.

Toph kicked it off the table.

“Hey.”

“No paperwork at dinner.”

“You teach students during breakfast.”

“Earthbending is a sacred art.”

“You threw a pebble into Penga’s porridge because she slouched.”

“Sacredly.”

Katara covered a laugh with her cup.

Aang looked between the four of us, too quiet in the way he became when an idea was forming.

I pointed my spoon at him. “Whatever you’re about to say, make it less terrifying than ‘we should talk.’”

“I learned from that.”

Toph snorted. “Barely.”

Aang rubbed the back of his neck. “What if we found a place together?”

The courtyard seemed to hold still.

Not because the question was shocking. We spent most nights in the same house already. My rented room had become an expensive storage closet containing two shirts, a chipped cup, and a landlord increasingly suspicious that I had died.

Still, living together was different from sleeping over.

Toph’s face went blank.

Katara’s did the opposite. Every feeling arrived at once: surprise, hope, worry, calculation.

I set down my spoon.

Aang hurried on. “Not because we have to. And not necessarily this house. I just thought—between the clinic, the academy, council work, and my travel, we keep trying to create home in the spaces between everything else.”

“That was almost good,” Toph said.

“Almost?”

“You used the word home like a poem.”

“I like poems.”

“I know. It’s exhausting.”

Katara touched Aang’s wrist. “I like the idea.”

Toph’s shoulders tightened.

Katara noticed. “The idea. Not a decision.”

That distinction mattered.

Toph leaned back on her hands. “If we live together, I need ground access.”

Aang nodded immediately.

“No second-floor bedroom where I have to guess what everyone’s doing through wood supports.”

“Okay.”

“And nobody moves my stuff because it’s ‘clutter.’”

Katara looked personally attacked.

“It is clutter when your shoes are in the stove.”

“They were drying.”

“They were smoking.”

“Same family of activity.”

I raised a hand. “I need a door that closes.”

Three faces turned toward me.

“A room?” Aang asked.

“Maybe. Or an office. Somewhere that is mine enough that I can close it and not be available.”

Katara nodded first. “Yes.”

I looked at her. “That was fast.”

“Because you don’t stop working until somebody physically removes the paper from your hands.”

Toph kicked my council packet farther away.

“Exhibit one.”

Aang’s smile softened. “I want roof access.”

Toph groaned.

“What?”

“You’re going to jump off it.”

“I’m an airbender.”

“That’s not a denial.”

Katara said, “I want a kitchen big enough for four people to be in without becoming a diplomatic incident.”

“We could just ban Toph.”

Toph pointed at Aang. “I know where you sleep.”

“That threat works better if we already live together.”

Toph’s grin widened.

The conversation lasted two hours.

It became less romantic as it continued, which made it more useful.

Money. Privacy. Guests. Who would own what. Whether the house would be tied to Aang’s public office. Whether Toph could legally install training posts in a dining room. Whether Katara would murder anyone who left wet towels on the floor.

“Yes,” she said.

I wrote that down.

Aang peered at my notes. “Did you actually write ‘murder’?”

“Documentation protects everyone.”

Toph laughed so hard she nearly fell off the bench.

The strangest part was how ordinary it felt.

I had expected love with the Avatar to be made of impossible things. Flights over mountains. Council chambers. Spirits. History moving under our feet.

Instead, we were arguing about cupboard space.

I loved it so much it frightened me.

That fear followed me home.

My rented room smelled stale when I opened the door. Dust had collected on the sill. A shirt hung over the back of a chair exactly where I had left it days ago. Nothing had changed because almost nothing happened here anymore.

I sat on the edge of the bed.

Moving in with them would mean giving up the last place that belonged only to me.

I had spent too much of my life understanding that belonging could become dependence, and dependence could become a trap if the wrong person held the key.

The next morning I told them.

Not elegantly.

“I need an exit.”

Aang stopped pouring tea.

Katara went still.

Toph’s head tilted.

I forced myself to continue. “If we do this, I need enough money kept separate that I could leave. I need my documents under my control. I need my own key. I need nobody to treat that like I’m planning to abandon you.”

Silence.

Then Toph slapped the table.

“Yes.”

I blinked.

She pointed at me. “That. More of that.”

Katara exhaled. “I agree.”

Aang set down the kettle. “So do I.”

Something in my chest loosened.

Aang sat across from me. “Being able to leave is part of choosing to stay.”

Toph grimaced. “Ugh. That was actually good.”

“Thank you.”

“I hate it.”

Katara reached over and took my hand. “We can make a household agreement.”

Toph groaned louder. “Sugar Queen discovered contracts.”

“You like contracts when they stop people from deciding things for you.”

“That is unfairly accurate.”

So we made one.

Not vows.

Not marriage papers.

A household agreement.

Separate money. Shared expenses. Private rooms when wanted. No reading each other’s correspondence without permission. No volunteering another person’s labor to public causes. No using bending to win household arguments.

Toph objected to the last rule.

“Then I get to use council procedure.”

She withdrew the objection.

Aang added a line that nobody could turn the home into an official Avatar residence without unanimous agreement.

Katara added that sick people were allowed to be sick without apologizing.

Toph added that help had to be offered, not imposed, unless someone was unconscious or actively on fire.

I added that nobody’s fear of being left could become a reason to prevent someone else from leaving a room, an argument, or the relationship.

We all signed.

Toph stamped her thumb in ink beside her name because she said signatures were pretentious.

Aang drew a tiny air swirl beneath his.

Katara rolled her eyes and then added a wave beneath hers.

I drew nothing.

Toph took the pen back and added a small square beside my name.

“What is that?”

“A filing cabinet.”

I stared at her.

She smiled sweetly.

Two weeks later, we found a house on a broad street near the eastern canal.

It was ugly.

Toph loved it immediately.

The foundation was old Earth Kingdom stone, solid enough for her to read half the block. The roof was flat. A narrow courtyard held a dead plum tree. The kitchen was enormous because the previous owner had run a noodle shop from it.

Aang climbed onto the roof before the agent finished speaking.

Katara opened every cabinet.

Toph walked barefoot through each room, tapping walls and announcing which repairs had been lied about.

I found a small room at the back with a window over the canal and a door that closed.

For a moment, I stood alone inside it.

The room was empty.

No desk. No shelves. No papers.

Still, I could see them.

I could see a lock on the drawer with my documents. A chair by the window. A place where my work ended because I decided it ended.

Aang appeared in the doorway but did not cross it.

“Yours?” he asked.

I looked around.

Then at him.

“Mine,” I said.

His smile was bright and easy.

“Good.”

He left me there without asking to come in.

That was when I knew I could live with him.

Not because he made room for me.

Because he understood that some rooms had to remain mine.

Home, I was learning, was not the place where nobody ever left.

It was the place where leaving a room did not threaten love.

It was the place we returned to because the doors opened both ways.
